extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of public administration/political science; municipal policymakers and reformers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and institutional rules for assessing the working and efficiency of city governments (services provided, cost, institutional design, causes of misgovernment) with illustrative examples from U.S. cities (Boston, New York, St. Louis, Philadelphia).

rubrics_metrics.name: Test — provision for the people
rubrics_metrics.description: What does the city provide for its inhabitants? (One of two tests of practical efficiency.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Space is insufficient for full detail, but common complaints include bad paving and cleansing of streets, non-enforcement of laws forbidding gambling and illicit drinking, poor control of the police, sanitary arrangements, and management of public buildings and parks. Comparison with certain European cities (Glasgow, Manchester, Dublin, Hamburg, Lyons) indicates American cities often fall short.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test — cost to the people
rubrics_metrics.description: What does the government cost the people? (Second test of practical efficiency: debt and taxation.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure debt and taxation levels (examples: increases in population, valuation, taxation, and debt across major US cities 1880–1905). Consider increases in funded debt and annual expenditures per inhabitant; distinguish permanent improvements from debt due to waste or malversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayor nomination and election procedure (Boston)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nominations for mayor: petitions signed by at least 5,000 qualified voters on official forms; signatures verified by affidavit; file with Election Commissioners at least 25 days before election; commissioners scrutinize and announce validly nominated names not less than 16 days before election; ballot without party designation; order of names by lot; municipal election date and fiscal year specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Official ballot contains names in lot-determined order, without party designation. Municipal election on Tuesday after second Monday in January; fiscal year begins first Monday in February.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayoral recall rules (Boston)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recall (dismissal) of the mayor: provision for recall at end of two years of a four-year term; recall conducted at regular State election and must secure a majority of total enrolled votes (not just polled votes); recall can be used only at the midpoint of the term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because majority of enrolled voters is required, about two-thirds of polled votes are typically necessary in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayoral powers and appointment/removal rules (Boston)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mayor appoints heads of city departments whose appointments are not otherwise provided for; mayor's appointments are not subject to council confirmation but require a certificate from the State Civil Service Commission that the appointee is qualified; mayor may remove any official at any time but must state in detail the specific reasons for removal; all recommendations for expenditure must originate with the mayor; mayoral veto of council resolutions is final.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Council may omit or reduce recommended items but cannot insert or increase any such item. Appointments without the State Civil Service certificate are not valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: City Council composition, nomination, powers and limitations (Boston)
rubrics_metrics.description: Council of nine members elected at large (not by wards) for three-year terms with three retiring annually; candidates nominated by petitions signed by at least 5,000 registered voters (filing and verification similar to mayor); names placed on official ballot in order by lot and without party designation; no provision for recall of councillors before term expiration; councillors paid an annual salary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Powers include making city ordinances, approving appropriations including the annual budget, authorizing loans and sanctioning certain multi-year contracts — all exercised subject to the mayor's veto. Authority to grant street privileges, franchises, permits and locations vested in a three-member street commission appointed by the mayor, though council with mayor's approval may fix general terms for such privileges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finance Commission (Boston) — investigative watchdog
rubrics_metrics.description: A body of five members appointed by the governor for five-year terms (one member retires annually); chairman paid $5,000 and other members $3,000; no mandatory or executive powers, but empowered to investigate matters relating to appropriations, loans, expenditures, accounts, and methods of administration and to report results to mayor, council, governor, and legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission may employ experts (up to $25,000/year), can compel attendance of witnesses and production of papers, but holds purely investigatory authority (no executive mandate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative departments — appointment and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: City administration conducted by about thirty departments, most with a single commissioner or a board of three; most department heads paid, a few boards unpaid; none elected or appointed by the council; nearly all appointed by the mayor with important exceptions (police commissioner and board of excise appointed by governor; Trustees of the Franklin Fund appointed by the State Supreme Court).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All judges, including municipal justices, are appointed by the State governor with confirmation by his Council.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metropolitan commissions for regional coordination
rubrics_metrics.description: Metropolitan commissions (appointed by the governor) coordinate services across multiple municipalities in a metropolitan district — e.g., Metropolitan Water and Sewerage Board handles main water supply and trunk sewers; Metropolitan Parks Commission maintains parks and boulevards; ad hoc commissions (Charles River Basin Commission, Boston Transit Commission) created for multi-municipality undertakings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composition and appointment vary (example: Boston Transit Commission composed of five members, three appointed by governor and two by the mayor).

rubrics_metrics.name: School Committee structure (Boston)
rubrics_metrics.description: Boston School Committee composed of five members elected at large for three years with provision for one or two members retiring each year; nomination and election rules similar to municipal councillors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: School administration treated as distinct from regular city administration; importance emphasized and vulnerability to machine/spoils methods noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board of Education reform (St. Louis model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 1897 St. Louis statute the Board of Education consists of twelve members chosen at large for six years with four members retiring every second year; each member swears to consider merit and fitness only in making appointments; board's functions chiefly supervisory while executive work is left to the superintendent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This arrangement is cited as having 'taken education out of politics' and raising efficiency of schools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause of municipal misgovernment — incompetent and unfaithful governing boards and officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Many important offices filled by men possessing little or no fitness; such unworthy office-holders gain places by exertion and promise unlawful emoluments and patronage, leading to dismissal of competent subordinates, creation of new places, profitable contracts, and needless public works; these unlawful demands enter estimates and lead to borrowing via bonds rather than immediate taxation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commissioners assert that more than one-half of present city debts may be the direct results of intentional and corrupt misrule; the description includes how anticipated gains, corrupt promises, and issue of bonds conceal and perpetuate corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause of municipal misgovernment — introduction of State and national politics into municipal affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Formation of general political parties and party machinery intrudes into municipal affairs where party differences are largely irrelevant; partisan control of municipal offices leads to patronage, organization of corrupt elements, dependency classes, and a paralysis of good-citizen cooperation for honest municipal government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Party strife makes it impossible for good citizens to unite on municipal issues; leading national figures keep forces in hostile array to retain patronage; many participants view politics as a livelihood rather than public service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause of municipal misgovernment — assumption by State legislature of direct control
rubrics_metrics.description: State legislative intervention in local affairs disregards municipal self-government, brings legislators without necessary time or knowledge to direct local affairs, leads to log-rolling of local bills, a multiplicity of conflicted statutes, legal uncertainty, and incessant litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative control also transferred methods of corruption to the State capitol, facilitating purchase of lands, grading/paving/sewering for corrupt contracts, compelled purchases at extravagant prices, creation/abolition or reallocation of offices to shift patronage, and extension of corrupt influence statewide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spoils system and party machinery as aggravating factor
rubrics_metrics.description: The Spoils system (office as reward for party service) and the party machinery that supports it are especially potent in great cities, encouraging patronage and corruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cities have many features that amplify spoils effects: large numbers of recent immigrants untrained in self-government, many voters who pay no direct taxes, and able citizens preoccupied with private business — all reducing effective civic resistance to corrupt machines.
